7. The defendant Nos. 1-4 entered appearance in the suit and filed a written statement denying the allegations in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation; that the agent of the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation had refused to load 10 trailors on board due to shortage of space but the shipper's agent/freight forwarder, compelled the agent of Bangladesh Shipping Corporation to load the same on deck; that the vehicles were found very old, broken and damaged in a tally made by the stevedores and the same was recorded by the Chief Officer of the vessel in the Daily Working Report; that although the commercial invoice, packing list and Clean Report of Findings by Inspectorate Griffith Limited states that all the 27 vehicles had been manufactured in the year 1995-96 evidence obtained from Ms Leyland Exports, Ms HASA (Export) Limited and British Car Numbers registration system covering motor vehicles prove that the cars imported by the plaintiff had been manufactured in the 1980's and that the plaintiff had imported banned vehicles into Bangladesh in violation of the Import Policy Order, 1997-2000. The defendants further contended that after loading of the goods on board the vessel, it sailed from Hull on 20-10-1999. The vessel encountered severe cyclone storm in the Bay of Biscay on 23-10-1999 and called at Southampton on 26-10-1999 for emergency repairs, re-stowage and re-lashing of cargo for safe prosecution of the rest of the voyage. The vessel resumed her voyage, on 6-11-1999. The defendants claimed that due to unforeseen weather conditions, which was an Act of God, the vessel had lost 14 days. After discharging Jeddah-bound cargo the vessel proceeded to her next port of call at Male. Due to the ongoing holy month of Ramadan the daily working hours at Male were reduced to almost half of the normal working hours as a consequence of which the vessel suffered a delay of 12 days at Male when the vessel arrived at Chittagong it had to stay at the outer anchorage for 13 days for getting a discharge berth due to severe port congestion prevailing at Chittagong port at the time. Further delay was encountered by the vessel due to the expiry of the vessel's cargo gear Jumbo Derrick fitness certificate. As a consequence the vessel could not sail from Chittagong for her next destined port at Mongla without renewal of the said certificate by the classification society, the Lloyds Register of Shipping. The vessel arrived at Mongla on 21-2- 2006 for discharging the Mongla-bound cargo. The defendants contended that in the Joint Survey Report the surveyors had not stated any significant structural damage to the second-hand vehicles. The defendants further contended that the deadline for commencing the proceedings in Bangladesh in accordance-with the order dated 10-9-2001 passed by the Court in Singapore expired on 10-1-2002, but the suit was filed on 12-1-2002 and hence the suit is barred by limitation and liable to be dismissed. 

 (iii) Is the suit barred by limitation? 

 40. Mr Masud R Sobhan, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff, submitted that the pre-shipment inspection agency Inspectorate Griffith (UK) Ltd had inspected the goods prior to shipment and issued the CRF Certificate dated 21-10-99 certifying that "the goods were in good condition with ten years of economic life. He referred to the bills of lading (Exhibit 4) issued by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation (BSC) where it was noted the goods were shipped on board in apparent good order and condition. He submitted that the vessel started her voyage on 21-10-1999 and arrived at Mongla after a period of 4(four) months whereas it takes only 15 days to reach Mongla from Hull. He argued that the damage to the goods had taken place when the same was in the custody and control of the defendants and that the defendants are liable to make good the loss and damage suffered by the plaintiff. He submitted that the BSC issued "Clean Shipped on Board" BS/I dated 20-10-1999 for the cargo in question, but loaded the cargo on deck in fundamental breach of the contract. He submitted that the fact the vessel had encountered severe storm in the Bay of Biscay and had to go back to Southampton for repair work on 26-10-1999 caused further damage to the goods which were carried on deck. Mr Sobhan referred to the suit filed by the plaintiff being admiralty in Rem No. 600196 of 2001 in the High Court of Singapore and submitted that the Court in Singapore passed the order on 10-9-2001 upon a sworn application made by the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and on its undertaking, inter alia that it would not rely on the time bar in the suit to be commenced in Bangladesh. He argued that 'limitation' cannot be pleaded as a defence iri view of the undertaking of the BSC as incorporated in the order of the Singapore High Court. Mr Sobhan further submitted that the defendant No. 2 by several letters induced the plaintiff not to come before 'this Court in time. He referred to Exhibit 7 and contended that the BSC had granted the plaintiff an extension of time in respect of the plaintiff's claim. He further submitted that the plaintiff filed the suit on 12-1-2002 but the defendants have taken a plea that the last date for filing the suit was 10-1- 2002 and accordingly the suit was time barred. In this regard Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, Advocate appeared on behalf of the plaintiff and argued that the 10th of January 2002 was a Thursday which is a holiday of this Court and that following day i.e. Friday was a regular government holiday. In this regard the learned Advocate referred to the provisions of section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1908. Mr Sobhan submitted that the documents (Ext-O series) exhibited by the defendants in support of the plea that the vehicles were manufactured in 1980 had been issued by an authority which had not seen/ inspected the vehicles and engine spare parts. He argued that Customs Authorities had released the goods after proper examination of the goods and the related documents and, as such, the argument is not tenable. Mr Sobhan referred to the decision in the case of Trans Oceanic Steamship Co Ltd vs Adamjee Insurance Co Ltd reported in 46 DLR 23, where the Court in interpreting Articles III and IV of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 had held that as soon as the shipper delivers goods to the carrier at the port of origin in good condition he is entitled to receive the goods at the port of destination in good condition and that the carrier will be held responsible for the loss or damage to the goods which are in his care and custody. It was further held that initial onus is on the shipper to show that he delivered the goods in good condition and received the same in damaged condition and then the onus is shifted on the carrier to prove that its employees took due care and caution as a reasonable man of ordinary prudence to protect the goods but in spite of their taking such action due to circumstances beyond their control such as perils of the sea, Act of God, etc the goods were damaged. 

 41. Mr M Hafizullahappearing with Mr Md Ohiullah, the learned Advocate for defendants, submitted that the vessel MV Banglar Kakoli arrived at the port of Mongla on 21-2-2000 and discharge of the cargo commenced on 22-2-2000 and was completed on 23-2-2000 whereas the plaintiff filed the instant suit on 12-1-2002. He argued that the period of limitation had expired on 23-2-2001. He referred to the admiralty suit being Admiralty in Rem No. 600196 of 2001 filed by the plaintiff in the High Court of Singapore and submitted that in the order dated 10-9-2001 passed by the Court in Singapore, it was specifically provided that in the event proceedings are not commenced in Bangladesh within 3 (three) months from the date of conditions as set out in paragraph 1 therein are complied with the Singapore action would be dismissed with costs. The plaintiffs did not commence proceedings in Bangladesh within the stipulated time and accordingly the Court in Singapore dismissed the action by order dated 25-1-2002. He submitted that in the circumstances the conditions that Bangladesh Shipping Corporation would not rely on the time bar would not apply to the defendants in the instant proceedings. He submitted that the plaintiffs have themselves admitted in paragraph 6 of the plaint that they took delivery of the cargo on 24-2-2000 whereas the instant suit has been filed on 12-1-2002 and accordingly the instant suit is barred by limitation and is liable to be dismissed since. In response to Mr Khan Saifur Rahman's argument that the 10th of January 2002 was a Thursday, which was a Court holiday and that the subsequent date i.e. the 11th of January 2002 being a Friday the period of limitation would run from the 12th of January 2002. Mr Hafizullah placed before the Court a notification dated 13-11-2001 issued by the Registrar of the Supreme Court issued under order of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh from which it appears that the Court hours as specified in the notification was 10-30 AM to 4-15 PM with a break from 1-15 PM to 2-00 PM and that the office hours on Thursday were shown to be from 9-45 AM to 2-00 PM. He argued that it is clear from the notification that the offices of the Court were open on Thursday from 09-15 AM to 2- 00 PM during which time the Court would carry on its normal work and that such work would include filling of suits and pleadings. Mr Hafizullah referred to the bills of lading issued by the BSC (Exhibit 1) and pointed out that by accepting the bills of lading the plaintiff had agreed to the conditions set out therein, particularly Clause 4 and clause 8 on the reverse side of the bills of lading. He referred to Article Ill, Rule 6 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 and argued that if any suit or proceeding is not commenced against the carrier within a period of one year from the date of discharge of the cargo the liability of the carrier is completely extinguished and the proceeding is liable to be dismissed forthwith. 

 "(1) All further proceedings herein be stayed on the following conditions: a) The defendants undertake to the plaintiffs-i) not to rely on time bar in the suit to be commenced by the plaintiffs in Bangladesh; ii) not to adopt in the Bangladesh proceedings the package limitation under the Hague Rules as applied by Bangladesh law but on condition that the defendants may rely on the limitation provisions applicable under the Hague Visby Rules as applied in Singapore and/or the tonnage limitation under the Singapore Merchant Shipping Act (Capt. 179) iii) if it is material not to take any point in the Bangladesh proceedings, which would put them in a more favourable position than under the HagueVisby Rules as applied in Singapore b) The defendants shall furnish security in the same wording as presently provided save that it shall also respond to a judgment or order of a Bangladesh Court in the sum of US$ 1 million or such other sum as may be finally determined by the Court 2) In the event proceedings are not commenced in Bangladesh by the plaintiffs in respect of the claim being the subject matter of this action within 3 months from the date the conditions set out in paragraph 1 are complied with, the said security provided by the defendants to the plaintiffs shall become null and void and the same shall be returned by the plaintiffs to the defendants forthwith on demand for cancellation and the action herein shall stand dismissed with costs to the defendants without further order. 3) The defendants be at liberty to proceed with the appeal made by way of Registrar's Appeal No. 600087 of 2001 filed on 28th May, 2001." 

 53. Since the proceedings initiated by the plaintiff in Singapore had been dismissed by the Court in Singapore by order dated 25th January, 2002, with costs due to default of the plaintiff to initiate proceedings in Bangladesh in time, the condition that Bangladesh Shipping Corporation would not rely on the limitation provisions under Hague Visby Rules as applied in Singapore and/or tonnage limitation under the Singapore Merchant Shipping Act would not apply to the defendants in the instant proceedings. 

 54. The third paragraph of Rule 6 of Article III of the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 refers to the period of limitation and reads as follows: 

 From Exhibit 5 which is the report issued by the James Finlay PLC dated 5-3-2000 it appears that the vessel arrived at Mongla on 21-2-2000. The vessel started discharging its cargo at Jetty No. 8 at 1000 hours on 22-2-2000. The discharge was completed at 7-30 hours on 23-2-2000. The plaintiff apparently took delivery of the goods on discharge of the same from the vessel. In accordance with the above provisions of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act the suit ought to have been filed within one year from the date of delivery of the cargo i.e. 22-2-2001. This suit having been filed on 12-1-2002, the same is clearly barred by limitation. 

 55. In this context reference is made to some of the decisions placed before this Court in respect of cases where the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 was applicable and the Courts held that the right to file a suit was extinguished after the one year period of limitation. In Gladstone Wyllie and Co Ltd vs Shahidi Trading Corporation Ltd reported in 10 DLR 307 it was held by the High Court Division that a ship is discharged from all liabilities under Rule 6 of Article 3 of the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 in respect of loss or damage of the goods unless the suit is brought within one year after the delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered. 

 56. In Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd vs Brestern Shipping Company Ltd reported in 1983 BLD 3 = 34 DLR 362 it was held by the High Court Division that a suit filed beyond one year is barred by limitation. In the said judgment it was stated as follows: . 

 59. The plaintiff had contended that the defendant No.2 had by its letter dated 14-2-2001 granted an extension of time (Exhibit 7) in respect of the plaintiff's claim. Although the letter dated 14-2- 2001 purports to grant a three-month extension with effect from 21-2-2001 in respect of the plaintiff's claim, it is not an acknowledgment of liability within the meaning of section 19 of the Limitation Act, inasmuch as the letter has been sent "without prejudice and without accepting any liability/claim whatsoever". The "three-month extension" given by the BSC is not enforceable in law. 

 60. From the above it is clear that the plaintiff's suit is barred by limitation and the right of the plaintiff to file the suit is extinguished and no longer in existence.
